templates.content:
<writing_samples>
<sample_1>
Book 1 Normal Text:

The sombre morning cleared as Maeve walked along the lane to Home Farm, as if God above had ordered all the angels to sweep the bad weather of yesterday away. It left a bright day with the blue sky pierced by mountains bigger than those of her native Wales, not that Cardiff had any mountains within the city bounds, but she had been on holiday to Snowdonia, staying in a lovely guesthouse at the foot of Mount Snowden.
In her experience, people who lived on mountains were good, down-to-earth people, ones you could trust. She hoped that was the case around here. While the settlement of Strathfulton was in a valley with the river Fulton running rapidly through, it was surrounded by bens, as she had learned to call them from the guidebook she had read on the train.
Gosh, the train had arrived at Strathfulton station less than twenty-four hours earlier, thrusting her into a wholly different world. And, not only that, but a murder had happened on the day of her arrival. Would the locals think that strange? As if she had brought the wicked ways of the lowlands with her?
Well, she didn’t have time to think about nonsense like that. She realised how rapidly she was walking, her legs stretching her skirt as she strode down the lane. Was she really in such a hurry? Wouldn’t Home Farm still be there if she turned up ten or twenty minutes later?
To force the point, she stepped off the road and onto a stile she found that led into rough grazing. She had planned to climb the stile and jump down into the great expanse on the other side, but something made her sit on it instead. She looked over the land she owned as the Countess of Strathfulton, wondering if it wasn’t her promised land.
Then, she pulled her pocket watch from her skirt and exclaimed loudly about being late for Morton, the factor. She jumped off the style and straight into some cow dung lurking under the fence. What, she wondered, was a cowpat doing on the far side of the fence, close to the road?
Thanking her lucky stars for the stout boots Mrs Morton had put her in, she wiped her left boot as clean as she could on the tufty grass, then raced off up the lane to look for Home Farm.
She found it just as a sharp shower made her pull the raincoat (provided by Mrs Morton) tighter against her. The farmhouse, in fact the whole of the steadings, seemed to fold into the lay of the land, as if designed for maximum concealment.
A stout man in a tweed suit with huge green gumboots stood by the wall that divided farmhouse from farmyard. His iron-grey hair and stern gaze towards her gave the impression that he didn’t take life in any way, but with total seriousness. Most people, while waiting for a boss who was running late, might relax a little, leaning against the wall. Morton, however, looked like the wall could lean on him for support.
“My great-great-grandfather built that wall, milady,” were the first words he said to her, making Maeve wonder if he kept encyclopaedic knowledge in his broad, flat head concerning every task completed upon the Strathfulton thirty-thousand acres going back at least four generations.
“And a very good wall it looks, too,” she replied. “You must be Morton.”
“I am he, milady.” His natural pomposity made Maeve want to smile, such that she had to fight to control her internal urge to break out into fits of laughter. She couldn’t do that because she was in charge now, meaning people looked up to her. Gosh, how life can change in an instant.

Book 1 Dialogue Text:

“And your husband?” Maeve felt butterflies as she went to the main point.
“Mr Hamilton is away on business, an extended trip, I’m afraid.”
“Really? How awkward for you.” Maeve had been in the police for a number of years, ever since leaving school. She knew how to translate such statements.
“When do you expect him back?”
“Oh, not for quite some time, Lady Strathfulton.” That meant a very long sentence, implying a serious crime, maybe several such crimes, creating a spree. She decided to probe a little more.
“It makes for a difficult time for the ladies of the house when the gentleman is away for an extended business trip, does it not?”
“Yes, it can be quite a strain.”
“I should mention…” Maeve paused, thinking her approach wrong. She had been about to mention the matter of the outstanding rent, but decided against at the last minute; this lady was taut and taut people tend to snap.
“Yes?”
“Ah, yes, what was it now?” Maeve wracked her brain for something to fit with the sentence that she had just started. “Yes, of course, silly me. I should mention that I am looking for a secretary and I wondered whether your daughter might be looking for something of a distinctly professional nature to occupy her time.”
“Well, I see, yes, that might be just the thing. However, the girl is only just eighteen.”
“As was I when I started in the police force.”
“I meant in terms of earning a considerable salary. I mean, the responsibility would be quite something with so much income quite suddenly.”
She was asking for a cut. Maeve was familiar with such conduct, not, thankfully, with the police, but in the backstreets of Cardiff it had been a regular occurrence, part of the fabric of city life.
“Do you have any idea of how we might be able to introduce some way of protecting the poor girl?” Maeve asked, knowing exactly what the next words would be.
“Well, no, but actually, maybe I do. Of course, I wouldn’t spend it, but perhaps you could split the salary into two equal halves and I become the caretaker for the second portion, which Fi might well be grateful for a little later on.”
“So, it would be half to your daughter and half to you?”
“Exactly.”
“Well, I see a slight problem with that. Fi will be learning to administer the wages and salaries for the estate, hence she will see the payments to you and wonder why.”
“Oh, I don’t think…”
“No, sorry to interrupt, Mrs Hamilton, but I’ve just had the most wonderful idea that would keep it from certain eyes. Instead of paying the wages to you, why don’t we just offset it against the rent on Castle House?”
She knew that wasn’t going to go down too well, but perhaps it was the perfect balance in terms of looking after the estate. Mrs Hamilton looked distinctly angry, but she was a realist and an opportunist, grabbing whatever was within reach at the time.
She nodded her head, as if only slowly following such clever manipulations.
The only problem with the whole scheme was that Maeve had absolutely no idea of Fi Hamilton’s capability to work as a secretary.

Book 1 Action Text:

“Hello Mrs Count,” she said when Maeve came across the playground and made her way towards the lane that led home.
To her new home. To Strathfulton Castle.
“Mrs…? Oh, I get it. Well, strictly it should be Miss Countess, my dear.”
“Hello, Miss Countess, did you see the body? I was the one who discovered it. I was going up to Mr MacGregor at his desk when I noticed how still he was, like. Then I touched him and see what happened?” She showed the sleeve of her cardigan. “It’s real blood, you know. Are you really the new countess, Miss? I never saw the last earl on account of him not being interested in a place like this, but, do you know what, he only got hung. I saw it in Dad’s newspaper. It said hanging is a cruel way to die. I can imagine it’s very painful, don’t you think? And why is it that the wife of an earl is a countess, yet…?”
“Wow, you’re quite the chatterbox, aren’t you? And I don’t even know your name, my dear.”
“Pudding.”
“What?”
“Well, that isn’t my birth name, but it’s what everyone calls me on account of being as round as a roly poly pudding.”
“It seems this little village has a tendency to being overweight,” Maeve said to whoever wanted to listen, as Pudding naturally fell into step beside her.
“Where do you live?” Maeve asked the young teenager.
“That’s a silly question, Miss Countess,” came the reply, which shook Maeve considerably.
“What…?”
“At the gatehouse, don’t I just? Me and Ma live…”
“Ma and I,” Maeve corrected gently.
“That’s what I said, isn’t it now?” Pudding’s habit of ending her sentences with a question was like a steaming cup of hot chocolate on a stormy afternoon.
Like today. The 3rd of June. The day Mr MacGregor’s life ended.
And their search for the killer began.
“No, Pudding dear, you need to get the grammar right.”
“I don’t have a grandma,” the girl replied, making Maeve realise that she wasn’t the only person struggling with an accent.
“You were saying?”
“Was I? Oh yes, Miss Countess, we live at the gatehouse, Ma and… I mean Ma and I, so we do.”
“You’re the gatekeeper? Or, your parents are?”
“That’s right, Miss Countess. No longer me dad as he’s gone on to another place, you see?”
“I’m so sorry to hear that, eh… Pudding. It must be sad for you to bear the loss.”
“Oh no,” she replied, “not that type of place at all. He went on the fishing boats and then wrote from Norway to say he had found someone else and wouldn’t be coming back. Ma almost burst with rage that day and I tried to tell Ma he wasn’t worth crying over. Now Mr MacGregor is a different bucket of fish altogether. Such a nice man.”
She started crying at that point, the tiny silent sobs that come before the sobs. Maeve drew the girl to her from instinct, putting both arms around her to keep the fear out.
Then, they both broke into a run, racing each other towards the castle, chased by the threat of yet another storm racing in from the Atlantic.
</sample_1>

<sample_2>
Book 2 Normal Text:

Instead, I carried twelve books on Egyptian pottery, three trowels of varying lengths, and zero plan for convincing Dr. Bradford that a woman could identify artifacts by more than just their "pretty colors."
My father's goodbye echoed in my head: "get Egypt out of your system, my dear girl, then return to New York to do the sensible thing!" By which he meant, marry Richard, his business partner's son—a fate I’d recently decided would be equivalent to being entombed with the pharaohs, minus the dignity of mummification.
I’d already managed several years ago to defeat Daddy’s objectives for me by training at Cambridge in England, a “silly notion for an American girl.” But he was still smarting over my recent defection from my engagement to Richard.
Steam cascaded across the tracks of Ramses Station—built thirty years ago as part of Khedive Ismail's grand modernization plan for Cairo and designed specifically to impress European visitors with Egypt's progress toward Western standards.
The vapor rolled over marble floors as I gripped my battered leather satchel, watching the throng surge around me like the annual flooding of the Nile. Except with significantly more bowler hats and fewer crocodiles. The morning light fractured through the train station's arched windows, casting honey-gold geometric patterns across the polished stone.
I had grossly miscalculated the weight of my research materials. The human body was not designed to transport so many books, no matter how essential they might be. As I attempted to wrangle my ungainly collection of luggage, a porter materialized at my elbow, rattling off a rapid string of Arabic.
I straightened my shoulders and deployed one of the few Arabic phrases I'd managed to memorize on the journey from London.
"Astatie 'an akil haqayibi."
And then questioned whether I'd just declared I could carry my own bags or accidentally proposed marriage. Based on his startled expression, it could have been either. Or something else entirely.
A socialite in an elaborate hat swept past, her perfume causing my eyes to water. Notes of henna (common in Egyptian perfumes since the Old Kingdom), vanilla (Madagascar origin, suggesting French colonial trade routes), and something that reminded me distinctly of a Cambridge colleague's failed attempt at brewing coffee using soil samples. My overdeveloped sense of smell was rarely a blessing, and often a curse.
The atmosphere vibrated with a symphony of sounds—vendors shouting prices in three languages and the mournful call to prayer echoing from distant minarets. The Cairo heat bore against my skin, and what felt like half of Cairo's population jostled my carefully pressed linen ensemble—selected to project professional competence and now transformed into a study in wrinkles during the train ride from Alexandria. At this rate, I'd arrive at the dig site looking less like a serious archaeologist and more like something recently excavated.
I made a brief stop at my prearranged lodgings, a narrow room above the Nile View Café, which notably had no discernible view of the Nile. My tiny upstairs room also smelled of aniseed and what I prayed was not decomposing camel.
I changed into my excavation attire. The outfit consisted of practical trousers (scandalous), a loose cotton shirt (sensible), and boots that had seen better days, possibly during the Old Kingdom period.
The mirror above the washbasin reflected a face I barely recognized. My reddish-blonde hair had escaped its pins during the journey, creating a halo of unruly waves to my shoulders, while the Egyptian sun seemed to have already intensified the freckles across my nose. Nondescript gray-green eyes looked back at me, bloodshot from the dusty train ride. I tucked away the lapis lazuli pendant I always wore, smoothed down my cotton shirt, and sighed. Not exactly the image of a respected academic, but then, appearances had never been my primary concern.

Book 2 Dialogue Text:

"I say, has someone mistaken this for a secretarial pool? This is a dig site, not a typing room."
I pivoted to find a cluster of men in various states of archaeological dishevelment. The speaker, a portly gentleman with an astonishing mustache, peered at me through a monocle that hadn't been cleaned since Rameses II was in nappies. My fingers instinctively twitched toward my field notebook, ready to document this remarkable specimen of Academicus pompousis.
Instead, I extended my hand. "Dr. Clarissa Bell. Cambridge University. My credentials arrived last week with Dr. Sutherland's recommendation." I'd counted on Sutherland's presence to ease the introductions, but he wasn't among them. His absence sent an uneasy prickle down my spine.
The mustache twitched. The monocle dropped. Several of his companions developed sudden, fascinating interests in their boot tops.
"Ah yes, Sutherland's... protégé." He managed to make the word sound like a particularly distasteful skin condition. "You don't look like an archaeologist.” His gaze flicked dismissively over my red-blonde hair and freckled skin. "I expected someone more... scholarly."
"I am sorry to disappoint."
"Hmm. Well. I am Dr. Nathaniel Bradford. I suppose you can help catalogue the pottery fragments coming out of G 3152. Sutherland's not here yet, which is most irregular." Bradford's voice carried a note of genuine concern that contradicted his dismissive demeanor. "But Phillips, my field photographer, can show you where to set up your... workspace." He flicked his hand toward a canvas tent that appeared to be losing an argument with the wind. "I shall introduce you around to the scholars later. We're all quite unavailable here at the moment."
Behind him, local workers navigated with practiced efficiency, their trowels creating a rhythmic tink-tink against limestone that sounded suspiciously like Morse code for "another foolish American." I noticed how they exchanged glances when I appeared—curious rather than dismissive—some even offering small nods of acknowledgment.
The dig site bristled with the tools of our trade: delicate brushes for cleaning, pointed trowels worn smooth by use, metal sieves that chimed like byzantine bells when the wind hit them right. My own toolkit, which I had ordered new from London, still gleamed with embarrassing brightness.
I smiled for Bradford, the way I imagined a sphinx might smile just before posing a riddle that ended in someone's gruesome death. "So kind of you." I nodded to each of the others. "And the team needs little introduction, as I've read all your work in preparation for joining you. I've published myself, on New Kingdom pottery classification systems. Perhaps some of you have read my work in the Journal of Egyptian Archaeology?"
Bradford's mustache performed a complicated maneuver that suggested extreme distress, possibly attempting to detach itself and scurry away to find a more enlightened host. "Yes, well. The pottery fragments are already broken, so they should suit your capabilities perfectly."
The words landed with all the subtlety of a tomb collapse. My jaw clenched involuntarily, teeth grinding together.
I retreated to my assigned table, keeping my spine rigid and my expression neutral, though internally I was cataloging every variety of academic condescension I'd encountered since my first day at Cambridge. This particular specimen ranked seventh on my scale of infuriating dismissals, somewhere between "Did you take notes for your husband?" and "Remarkable insight—did one of the professors help you with that?"
I devoted the next hour to sorting through pottery relics that looked about as exciting as my great-aunt Gertrude's china collection. If Gertrude had taken a hammer to it and buried it in the desert for several millennia. The work itself wasn't beneath me; the problem was that I could see the real excavation happening fifty yards away, where the men were carefully uncovering what appeared to be a previously undocumented structure.
Their trowels moved in practiced synchronization, scraping away years of sand while brushes swept clean any promising surfaces. String grids divided the ground into neat squares, while spirit levels balanced on surfaces ensured that even gravity was properly documented.
The pottery fragments that were spread before me formed a constellation of broken history, each one catching the light differently.
My fingertips traced the uneven surface of a sherd, feeling the ridges where an ancient craftsman's fingers once pressed into soft clay, creating a tactile connection across thousands of years. Each ceramic fragment had its own story to tell.
"What secrets have you been keeping, you poor broken thing?" I whispered to a particularly interesting sherd. "Did they toss you aside, once you weren't perfect anymore?"
A gust of wind sent my carefully arranged sherds skittering across the table. I lunged to catch them, nearly upending my rickety wooden chair in the process. "Oh, for the love of Tutankhamun's underpants—“ My hand quivered as I scrambled to prevent the loss of an hour's meticulous sorting.
"Three-point-two meters per second, with a northeasterly vector of precisely forty-seven-point-five degrees, accounting for local thermal variations."
I glanced up to find that one of the team, Dr. Étienne Deveraux, had slipped beside my table with the efficiency of a well-dressed ghost. He was lanky and precise, with rimless spectacles perched on a narrow nose and fingers as delicate as the instruments he wielded. He held an anemometer in one hand and a leather-bound notebook in the other. The newest addition to Bradford's team had already gained a reputation for turning every excavation into an exercise in geometric perfection that would have made Pythagoras weep with joy. His jodhpurs remained mysteriously immaculate, as if he'd somehow convinced the desert to avoid sullying his Parisian tailoring.
"The wind speed." He extracted a set of silver calipers from his leather case with the reverence of a priest handling sacred relics. "Fascinating how it affects artifact displacement. That ceramic fragment—“ he indicated with his polished pencil, “—must have traveled 50 centimeters before you caught it." He made another neat notation in his journal, the numbers marching across the page in perfect formation.
"How terribly useful." I pulled out my own notebook. "I've been meaning to calculate the exact aerodynamic properties of pottery sherds. Perhaps we could co-author a paper: 'Windblown Antiquities: A Mathematical Analysis of Archaeological Inconvenience.'"
I reached for the errant ceramic fragment, but Deveraux was already placing it back in line.
Dr. Bradford appeared, his other companions clustered behind him like a Greek chorus of disapproving mustaches and sand-dusted tweeds.
"Deveraux's not bothering you, I hope, Miss Bell?" He tugged at his too-tight collar.
I straightened. "Not at all. I was just noting the unusual fabric composition of this sherd. The inclusion of calcium carbonate suggests⁠—"
"Yes, yes." Bradford waved his hand as if shooing away an annoying insect. "Just sort them by size and color. That should be simple enough, even for a..." He paused, his face contorting. "...lady archaeologist."
I felt something crack in my professional facade.
I had worked twice as hard as any man to earn my position, only to discover that in the end, it was my father's checkbook rather than my dissertation that had opened the door. His funding of the dig had secured my place on this expedition—a fact that burned like desert sun.

Book 2 Action Text:

"Yes, apparently it was. Because if one is going to destroy a priceless artifact, one might as well destroy one that's central to the dig director's research.
I briefly considered mummification as a preferable alternative to facing Bradford's reaction.
The worst part wasn't Bradford's rage or my colleagues' silent judgment—it was the naked vulnerability of public failure.
I stood amid the pottery pieces, mentally composing my own funerary text. "Here lies Clarissa Bell, who survived twenty-six years of life only to be murdered by an angry archaeologist with a surprisingly violent mustache. May Anubis judge her heart lightly, as her brain was clearly missing to begin with."
Heat crawled up my neck, determined to reach my cheeks.
Bradford’s face progressed through several fascinating colors, finally settling on a shade of purple that would have delighted any ancient Egyptian dye-maker.
"Do you realize what you've done?” Each word enunciated as if speaking to a particularly dim child.
Behind Bradford, several Egyptian workers exchanging knowing glances.
I looked at the pottery sherds, then back at him. "Created a practical exercise in archaeological reconstruction?"
The gathered crowd of archaeologists collectively inhaled.
Bradford straightened his jacket and touched his credentials hanging around his neck.
"Miss Bell," he managed through clenched teeth, "I believe your... talents... might be better suited to literally anywhere else in Egypt. Preferably somewhere far from any breakable artifacts. Perhaps you could study the migration patterns of sand?"
A hot desert breeze swept across the dig, carrying dust devils that swirled around my feet. I opened my mouth to point out that sand migration was actually a fascinating geological process essential to site preservation, but a flash of movement caught my eye. Beyond Bradford's shoulder, half-hidden in the shadows of the entrance to tomb G 3152, a figure stood watching our little drama unfold.
Unlike the other men on site, he wore no academic tweeds or archaeological kit, but rather an elegantly cut Savile Row sort of suit that seemed to defy the desert sun. His perfectly knotted tie suggested both taste and wealth. And he was holding something—something that glinted like gold in the harsh light.
The man noticed my attention. His subsequent smile contained the precise combination of charm and danger that archaeological instinct warned should be cataloged under Exhibits: Absolutely Do Not Touch. Something about his posture—the casual confidence of someone who navigated the world without permission.
I frowned. Unauthorized access to tomb sites was strictly forbidden, and that man had definitely not been part of our excavation team. Unless, of course, Bradford was in the habit of hiring aristocratic-looking strangers in bespoke suits to lurk in doorways.
Then he slipped into the tomb's darkness, taking whatever he'd been holding with him.
"Miss Bell!" Bradford's voice cut through my thoughts. "Are you even listening?"
No, I was not, in fact, listening. I was too busy wondering why a well-dressed stranger would be sneaking around our dig site—and why he'd looked so damnably pleased about my spectacular failure.
CHAPTER THREE

No one else seemed to have noticed the stranger, so I followed him down into the tomb, boot heels echoing against limestone. The sensible thing would be to alert Bradford—though he'd likely diagnose me with a case of feminine archaeological hysteria, a condition apparently brought on by allowing women too close to ancient artifacts.
I cataloged my options:
Option A: Alert Bradford (Common Resolution, Colonial Period, known to cause severe academic apoplexy)
Option B: Follow suspicious stranger alone into dark tomb (Rare Example of Archaeological Idiocy, Modern Period)
Option C: Pretend I hadn't seen anything (Cowardice, Well-Preserved Example of Career Preservation)
After my spectacular contribution to pottery destruction this morning, I couldn't risk being wrong. Consorting with an unauthorized visitor could jeopardize the dig's permissions—career suicide served with a side of professional humiliation.
The tomb's blackness pressed around me, heavy with four thousand years of dust and rather more recent bat deposits.
If he claims to be lost, I'll cite regulation 7B regarding unauthorized site access. If he's a thief, I'll... My mind stuttered. What exactly did one do with a tomb robber? None of my courses at Cambridge had covered "Confronting Well-Dressed Criminals 101." Perhaps they should have taught it, given archaeology's tendency to attract the aristocratically larcenous.
A flicker of movement ahead gave me pause. The stranger's silhouette was bent over something, and in his hand, that same golden glint I'd spotted earlier.
My heart performed an acrobatic flutter. First day on the job, and I might catch my own tomb robber!
I should get reinforcements.
No. I squared my shoulders. I hadn't spent six years studying Egyptian archaeology to falter now. If I returned with Bradford, only to find nothing amiss, I'd be relegated to sorting pottery by color and size for the remainder of my natural life—possibly even in the afterlife, where I'd no doubt be assigned 365 ushabti figurines, one for each day of eternity.
</sample_2>

<sample_3>
Book 3 Normal Text:

The bed beneath me jolted, waking me from a deep slumber. Only then did I hear the frantic pounding.
“Kitty. Are you awake?” My brother Ned. Outside my train compartment.
Heavens!
In a panic, I gazed bleary-eyed at the traitorous clock that was supposed to wake me at five. It was now past six.
“Kitty!”
Scrambling to my feet, I dived for the door and thrust it open to find my outraged brother on the other side. He was immaculately attired in a tailored, three-piece business suit, not a hair out of place.
I, on the other hand, was a rumpled mess in disheveled bedclothes and flyaway mane. Of course I was. I’d barely slept.
“We’re due in Paris in an hour, and you’re not dressed!”
“I’m sorry.”
“Did you forget to set your alarm?”
“Of course not. I would never do that.” Not when I knew he worshiped the god of punctuality.
“It didn’t go off?” He sounded incredulous.
I’d be as well. After all, my Jaeger-LeCoultre travel clock was one of the best in the world, so the fault could not lie with the timepiece, but with me. “I probably slept through it.” There was no probably about it. I had. But was it really my fault? On a night when I hadn’t dropped on the berth ‘til after midnight, there was no hope I’d awaken on time.
“Kitty.” Disappointment laced the word.
Only one way out of this sticky wicket. To dress as quickly as I could. “It won’t take me but a tick to get ready.” Thankfully, I’d set out my traveling clothes last night. “I won’t take long. I promise.”
All I got in return was a highly disapproving frown. It did not display him to advantage.
With no time to waste, I fetched my sage and lavender frock, silk stockings and undergarments—all in the height of fashion, of course—and stumbled past him in nothing but my nightgown and slippers. Praying that the lavatory was unoccupied, I rushed toward it, earning only one disapproving ‘harumph’ from a passing matron. I had to admit I’d earned that. After all, a lady doesn’t dash about in her undergarments in a public setting.

Book 3 Dialogue Text:

“Of course not.” He took my drawing pencil and wrote out a large H, small e and m, along with the rest of his name.
“Hold on to that,” James said, dropping a hand on Hem’s shoulder. “This lad will be famous one day. He’s a hell of a writer.”
“I’ll be on the lookout then.” I meant it. “Good night, gentlemen.”
“Good night,” they both said.
I headed down the long corridor, only turning around to look back after I reached the lift. The two were no longer where I left them. They’d probably gone back to the bar. I glanced at the sketch I’d drawn of Hem and noted his full name. Ernest Hemingway. It had a nice ring to it.
It was now close to eleven, a good time to tuck into bed. But I was too enervated by the encounter with the two writers to sleep. That mystery novel would help me unwind, though.
After I’d stepped off the lift, a conversation drifted toward me from the hallway on the right, one I would have to pass on the way to my room. A woman and a man, arguing. The woman’s tone reminded me of Rose Trevvyan.
In the next moment, my guess was confirmed. “Rose. Why are you doing this?”
“Money, darling, why else?” Her voice came across peevish, as if she resented his question.
“We have enough,” he said.
“You fool,” she barked out. “It’s never enough. I’m not going back to being poor again.”
“But why are you demanding money from him? Why Ned Worthington?”
I gasped. Was she blackmailing Ned? No wonder he was so perturbed when we ran into her.
“Because he’s rich, and he’ll pay,” Rose answered.

Book 3 Action Text:

“He’s rich.”
“Disgustingly so, I imagine.”
His lips twitched, but he didn’t say a word. But then he didn’t have to. The prospective client was probably richer than King Midas.
The train lurched and signs of civilization—buildings, houses, people—drifted by outside our window. “We should arrive soon.”
“Yes.” He leaned forward. “There’s one more thing I wished to discuss, Kitty. Your settlement.”
“Oh?” Father settled funds on my siblings when they turned one and twenty. Since I would celebrate that august birthday in a matter of weeks, the expectation was not foreign to me. Still, I was half afraid of what Ned would say. I hadn’t exactly been a model young woman. Maybe Father thought to withhold the money until he felt I’d matured.
“You’ll have access to your funds, at least some of them, on your birthday.”
I silently breathed a sigh of relief. “That’s good to know.”
He cleared his throat. “But Father won’t be managing them. I will.”
“You?” When Margaret turned one and twenty, it was Father she’d dealt with.
He reclined against the seat. “I asked Father if I could take on that responsibility, and he agreed.”
“Why would you want to?”
“The business has grown, especially this last year. We have clients not only from Britain, but France, Germany, the United States. It would be one less thing for him to worry about.”
I had a million questions about my settlement, but before I had a chance to ask them, the conductor knocked on our door. “Madame, Monsieur. We’re pulling into the gare de Lyon à Paris. Gather your items, s'il vous plaît.”
“Thank you,” Ned said before turning to me. “I’ve organized a car and a chauffeur to meet us outside the station. He’ll be at our disposal for the next two days.”
Clearly, questions about my settlement would have to wait until a more propitious time. “That’s brilliant.”
He came to his feet. “I’ll fetch my bags. Stay here until I return.”
Ever the protector. Something for which I was grateful, even if he went a little overboard at times. “I will. Thank you, Ned.”
His brow scrunched. “Whatever for?”
“For taking such good care of me. I do appreciate it.”
“Anytime, minx. What are brothers for?” he said, before stepping into the corridor.
Once more alone, I gazed out the window at the passing vista. Before long, we entered the station and the compartment grew dark. What would Paris bring? Plenty, as it turned out.

<style_guide>
Here is a comprehensive prose style sheet based on the provided writing samples. This guide is designed to instruct an LLM to replicate the specific tone, structure, and narrative techniques found in the text.

Historical Mystery Prose Style Sheet

1. Point of View (POV) and Tense

The writing style alternates between Third Person Limited and First Person Central, depending on the specific narrative need. However, the overarching rule is Deep POV in Past Tense.

Primary Tense: Past Tense (walked, saw, felt, said).

POV Options:

Option A (Third Person Limited): Focus strictly on one character per scene. The narrator knows only what the focal character knows and feels. (See Sample 1).

Option B (First Person): intimate, conversational, and highly internal. The narrator speaks directly to the reader, often with wit or retrospection. (See Samples 2 & 3).

Constraint: Do not "head-hop." Stay firmly anchored in the protagonist’s head. Do not describe the protagonist from the outside unless they are looking in a mirror.

2. Deep Point of View & Internalization

The narrative must filter all descriptions, events, and observations through the specific personality, background, and mood of the protagonist. The narrator should not sound like a neutral observer; the narration is the character thinking.

Filter the World through Expertise: Metaphors and similes should reflect the character's background (e.g., an archaeologist compares a person to a specimen; a police officer analyzes statements).

Example: "My fingers instinctively twitched toward my field notebook, ready to document this remarkable specimen of Academicus pompousis." (Sample 2)

Example: "Maeve had been in the police for a number of years... She knew how to translate such statements." (Sample 1)

Internal Monologue: Embed questions and exclamations directly into the narration to show the character's thought process.

Example: "What, she wondered, was a cowpat doing on the far side of the fence, close to the road?" (Sample 1)

Example: "If he claims to be lost, I'll cite regulation 7B... If he's a thief, I'll... My mind stuttered." (Sample 2)

Emotional Coloring: The environment should reflect the character's internal state.

Example: "The sombre morning cleared... as if God above had ordered all the angels to sweep the bad weather of yesterday away." (Sample 1)

3. "Show, Don't Tell" (Sensory & Action)

Avoid stating emotions directly (e.g., "she was nervous"). Instead, use physical reactions, sensory details, and interaction with the environment to convey feeling.

Physical Manifestations of Emotion:

Instead of "She was anxious about asking," use: "Maeve felt butterflies as she went to the main point." (Sample 1)

Instead of "I was embarrassed," use: "Heat crawled up my neck, determined to reach my cheeks." (Sample 2)

Environmental Interaction: Characters should interact with props and the setting during conversation or thought processes.

Example: "To force the point, she stepped off the road and onto a stile..." (Sample 1)

Example: "I gripped my battered leather satchel... The Cairo heat bore against my skin..." (Sample 2)

Sensory Specificity: Use specific smells, sounds, and textures.

Example: "Notes of henna... vanilla... and something that reminded me distinctly of a Cambridge colleague's failed attempt at brewing coffee using soil samples." (Sample 2)

4. Tone, Voice, and Humor

The narrative voice is intelligent, educated, and often witty or self-deprecating. Even in serious situations, there is a layer of "plucky" observation.

Witty Hyperbole: Use exaggeration for comedic or dramatic effect.

Example: "...a fate I’d recently decided would be equivalent to being entombed with the pharaohs, minus the dignity of mummification." (Sample 2)

Example: "Morton, however, looked like the wall could lean on him for support." (Sample 1)

Self-Deprecation: The protagonists often mock their own disheveled states or mistakes.

Example: "I, on the other hand, was a rumpled mess in disheveled bedclothes and flyaway mane." (Sample 3)

Period-Specific Phrasing: Use vocabulary that evokes a historical (likely early 20th century) British or Trans-Atlantic feel without being archaic. Words like "gosh," "stout," "rumpled," "sticky wicket," "propitious," and "apoplexy" help set the tone.

5. Dialogue Style

Dialogue should drive the plot while revealing class differences and personal relationships.

Action Beats over Tags: Minimize "he said/she said." Instead, use a sentence of action or description before or after the dialogue to attribute the speaker.

Example: "Yes, it can be quite a strain." / "I should mention…" Maeve paused, thinking her approach wrong. (Sample 1)

Example: "Do you realize what you've done?” Each word enunciated as if speaking to a particularly dim child. (Sample 2)

Class and Accent markers: If a character is from a different background, reflect this in their syntax (but use phonetic spelling sparingly).

Example (Lower Class/Rural): "At the gatehouse, don’t I just? Me and Ma live..." (Sample 1)

Example (Upper Class/Pompous): "Ah yes, Sutherland's... protégé. You don't look like an archaeologist." (Sample 2)

Interruptions and Internal Reaction: Characters often think about what they are hearing before responding, or they interrupt one another.

Example: "Really? How awkward for you." Maeve had been in the police... She knew how to translate such statements. (Sample 1)

6. Narrative Structure and Lists

The prose often employs distinct structural choices to organize the protagonist's chaotic thoughts.

Mental Lists: The narrative occasionally breaks into lists to show analytical thinking or sarcasm.

Example:
"I cataloged my options:
Option A: Alert Bradford...
Option B: Follow suspicious stranger..." (Sample 2)

Parentheticals: Use parentheses or dashes to insert quick, witty clarifications or sarcastic asides.

Example: "The outfit consisted of practical trousers (scandalous), a loose cotton shirt (sensible)..." (Sample 2)

7. Readability and Mechanics

Text Average Grade Level: 7th – 9th Grade.

Reasoning: The vocabulary is sophisticated (encumbrance, enunciated, pomposity) but the sentence structure is fluid and accessible.

Sentence Variance: Mix long, flowing sentences describing the setting with short, punchy sentence fragments for internal realization.

Example: "Like today. The 3rd of June. The day Mr MacGregor’s life ended." (Sample 1)

Summary Checklist for the Writer (LLM)

Is the POV deep? Are we hearing the character's internal voice and biases?

Is the setting active? Are characters interacting with props (stile, pottery, train door) while talking?

Is the tone witty? Have you included a metaphor related to the character's job or situation?

Is the period flavor present? Did you use words like "Gosh," "stout," or "rumpled"?

Did you show, not tell? Did the character feel "heat crawling up their neck" instead of "embarrassment"?
</style_guide>

templates.name: 1920s Historical Cozy Mystery Tropes
templates.content:
Major Tropes

The Amateur Sleuth

Your protagonist is the anchor of the story.

They are an everyday person without a badge or official training. In the 1920s setting, this usually means someone with a flexible profession—think journalists, typists, or society hostesses.

This gives them unique access to everything from high-society garden parties to gritty speakeasies.

Since they don't have forensic labs or authority, these characters rely on keen observation and social maneuvering. They solve crimes by decoding social cues or eavesdropping on servants that the upper class ignores.

Usually, they stumble into a murder by circumstance, perhaps at a country estate or on a train.

And because the police are often portrayed as incompetent or bound by red tape, your sleuth has to step up.

They are driven by a personal stake, like clearing a friend's name or protecting a family secret. It’s about intellect over brawn, using their unique position in the social flux of the Roaring Twenties to outwit the villain.

Appearance vs. Reality

The 1920s were a time of glistening surfaces covering up deep rot.

And for your story to work, you need to lean into that.

This trope relies on the tension between public respectability and private desperation. A wealthy businessman might actually be embezzling to cover gambling debts. A pristine widow might be surviving on blackmail.

It’s all about the façade.

You want to construct layers of deception where characters actively perform roles. The killer often appears to be the most trustworthy person in the room, perhaps a suitor using romance as camouflage or a "gentle" soul using poison—a method that looks natural but requires cold calculation.

And don't forget class lines.

Wealthy characters often benefit from assumptions of integrity, while servants are ignored. Use this. Your amateur sleuth should find the truth by listening to those the upper class deems invisible.

Ultimately, the unmasking shouldn’t just reveal the killer. It should reveal the gap between who they pretended to be and the ruthless person they actually are.

The Incompetent Police

This trope serves a critical function in your story.

It creates the necessity for your amateur sleuth to take charge.

The goal is to establish active barriers that prevent the professionals from solving the case too quickly.

And the 1920s provides plenty of historical justification for this.

In the US, Prohibition created a jurisdictional nightmare that overwhelmed local forces with bootlegging cases. In the UK, forensic technology was practically nonexistent, with fingerprinting still largely manual and unreliable.

So, lean into these constraints.

Show the police as underfunded, distracted by other crimes, or bound by strict departmental procedures that slow them down.

These systemic limitations create a gap that only your protagonist can fill.

While the police are stuck filing paperwork or chasing the obvious suspect, your sleuth uses her social connections to find the truth.

She succeeds not because the law is foolish, but because she has access that a badge can't buy.

Closed Circle Mystery

This constitutes the bread and butter of the genre.

The concept is simple but effective: you confine your suspects to a limited, isolated location.

And you need to make sure there is no escape.

For a 1920s setting, this usually involves a British country manor or a remote estate. You then apply a period-appropriate isolator, such as a raging snowstorm, a washed-out bridge, or cut telegraph lines.

This forces the killer to be one of the people in the room.

By limiting your cast to about 6 to 10 suspects—usually a mix of upper-class guests and "invisible" servants—you turn the story into an intellectual puzzle rather than an action thriller.

Everyone should be interconnected through existing family ties or hidden rivalries.

And because the police can’t reach them, the tension relies entirely on interpersonal friction and the terrifying realization that the murderer is sitting right across the dinner table.

The Red Herring

You can't have a 1920s mystery without misdirection.

The Red Herring is the primary tool used to keep your reader guessing until the very end.

And the secret to effective misdirection lies in the era itself.

In the 1920s, almost everyone had something to hide. To make this work, you need to give innocent suspects their own unrelated secrets that create suspicious behavior. Perhaps a character lacks an alibi not because they were committing murder, but because they were sneaking off to a speakeasy, concealing a gambling debt, or hiding a scandalous affair.

They have the appearance of guilt, but for the wrong reasons.

You should aim to layer two or three of these distractions early in the story.

Use era-specific details to sell the deception. This could be a nervous housekeeper hiding smuggled gin or a young heir prone to erratic episodes of shell shock.

This forces your sleuth to sift through layers of social deception.

Ultimately, the goal is to create a puzzle where the innocuous truth is buried under a mountain of lies. The suspense comes from distinguishing the social sins from the actual crimes.

Inherited Trouble

This is the perfect inciting incident to drag your protagonist out of their normal life and into the mystery.

It usually starts with a letter, a solicitor, or a summons regarding a distant relative.

But in the 1920s, an inheritance is rarely a blessing. It is almost always a curse.

You want to use this trope to physically move your amateur sleuth into the "closed circle," likely a decaying manor house filled with greedy relatives who were cut out of the will.

And this setting is ripe for conflict.

Because of the economic instability following WWI, estates are often riddled with debt or propped up by illicit Jazz Age schemes like bootlegging. When your protagonist arrives, they shouldn't just find a fortune; they should unearth long-buried family secrets.

Think illegitimate children, wartime affairs, or forged documents.

Your goal here is to create a pool of suspects—cousins, uncles, siblings—who all have a financial motive for murder. And since your protagonist is the outsider receiving the windfall, they are the only one with the perspective (and the lack of baggage) to see through the family lies and solve the crime.

The Modern Woman

The 1920s were defined by shifting gender dynamics.

And your protagonist needs to embody that shift.

She isn't just a set of bobbed hair and knee-length skirts; she is a functional tool for your plot.

Usually unmarried and financially self-reliant, she holds a job as a journalist, typist, or shop owner. This gives her the mobility to travel, drive, and enter male-dominated spaces like speakeasies without a chaperone.

But it also creates necessary friction.

Traditionalists will dismiss her as a "flapper upstart," which allows you to amplify the conflict with suspects.

While the police are stuck following procedure, she uses her independence to navigate the social landscape. She relies on female intuition to decode social cues that men miss.

And if there is romance? Keep it secondary to the mystery.

Her empowerment comes from her wits, not her suitors.

Poison as the Murder Method

Poison is the preeminent weapon of choice for the Golden Age mystery.

And for good reason.

It turns murder into an intellectual puzzle rather than a gruesome display of violence.

In the 1920s, regulations were surprisingly loose compared to today. Your villain doesn't need a black-market connection; they just need a garden or a rat problem. Common substances like arsenic or strychnine were readily available at the local chemist.

This accessibility is key.

Because symptoms often mimic common illnesses—like gastric distress or a heart condition—the discovery of the crime is delayed.

This gives your killer time to secure an alibi while the poison does its work.

So, lean into the domestic nature of the era.

Slip the dose into a gin cocktail, a calming bromide powder, or a shared pot of tea.

This forces your sleuth to rely on timelines and opportunity rather than ballistics, making it the perfect tool for a battle of wits.

Romance as a Subplot

You need to position the romance firmly in the backseat.

The central mystery always comes first.

And for the 1920s cozy mystery, this means keeping things subtle and chaste. We are talking about lingering glances and witty banter rather than graphic intimacy. The tension should arise naturally from the social shifts of the era, like the clash between the "modern woman" and traditional expectations.

But it must serve the plot.

Use the romantic interest as an ally or even a distraction, but never let the romance solve the mystery for you. That violates the fair-play rules of the genre.

Instead, I recommend treating the romance as a slow burn across a series.

Start with a professional partnership or polite flirtation in book one. Then, introduce era-specific obstacles like class distinctions or war trauma to create friction. Ultimately, the romance should add emotional stakes and act as a generator for red herrings, without ever overshadowing the intellectual puzzle.

Class Distinctions

Class isn't just setting dressing; it is a structural tool for your investigation.

Especially regarding the "invisible" servant.

Upper-class characters often speak freely in front of staff because they simply don't regard them as real people.

And you need to exploit this.

Your amateur sleuth can be in the room when the murder is planned, simply because she is pouring the tea.

But you must respect the hierarchy.

A housekeeper has legitimate reasons to inspect a guest's bedroom and find the hidden will. A kitchen maid does not.

Use these restrictions to control exactly what information your protagonist can access.

Furthermore, don't forget the financial anxiety of the era.

Post-war taxes were bleeding the aristocracy dry, and the middle class was terrified of losing their status.

This means your wealthy suspects often have the strongest motive of all: they are secretly broke.

While the police are blinded by the suspect's title or social standing, your sleuth uses her position to see the desperation behind the veneer.

Fish Out of Water

This is an incredibly effective tool for the 1920s setting.

Essentially, you want to drop your protagonist into an environment where they don't know the unwritten rules.

Think of an urban working-class girl suddenly navigating a Long Island mansion party, or a naive outsider entering a gritty speakeasy.

This highlights the rigid social hierarchies of the era.

But it serves a functional purpose for your plot, too.

Because they are an outsider, they aren't blinded by the social contract that binds the suspects.

While the elite guests are busy maintaining appearances, your protagonist is free to notice the servants' gossip or the subtle inconsistencies in a bootlegger's story.

I recommend triggering this with a displacement event, like inheriting a contested estate or chaperoning a wild relative.

This forces them into the "closed circle."

And while they might fumble the etiquette, their lack of ingrained respect for the upper class allows them to ask the blunt questions that actually solve the case.

The Stern Housekeeper

She is the ultimate gatekeeper of the domestic sphere.

Think of a middle-aged widow in black bombazine with a starched cap, pursed lips, and a glare that could stop a flapper in her tracks.

Her primary role is to serve as a domestic antagonist to your modern amateur sleuth. She represents the old guard, enforcing rigid class hierarchies and traditional rules that your protagonist is likely breaking just by existing.

And you want to use that friction.

While she creates obstacles—locking pantries, misplacing evidence like a poisoned teacup, or withholding gossip—she is also a goldmine of information. Because she has served the family for decades, she knows where the bodies are buried.

This makes her the perfect red herring.

But don't make her the killer. Instead, use her as a reluctant ally who eventually cracks to reveal the vital clue that breaks the case wide open.

Secret Passages

Everyone loves a hidden door behind a bookshelf.

But in a 1920s mystery, this isn't just about coolness; it is about architecture.

You want to place these in the aging family estates common to the genre, utilizing historical elements like priest holes or smuggler's tunnels. Even Prohibition-era modifications for bootlegging work well here.

But there is a rule.

You get one.

Golden Age "fair play" dictates that you limit yourself to a single secret passage so the reader can deduce its existence without feeling cheated.

Use it to facilitate the "impossible crime." It allows the killer to enter a locked room, poison the victim, and vanish.

Just make sure your sleuth finds it through her own keen observation—like noticing a draft or uneven floorboards—rather than dumb luck. That is how you reward the reader.

Dying Confession

This trope offers the ultimate narrative closure.

The premise is simple. The villain admits to their crimes, motives, and methods moments before their death.

And this serves a very specific function.

It allows you to skip the boring legal proceedings of a formal trial.

But why would a villain confess instead of fight for their life?

Because they have passed the point of no return.

Realistically, survival instinct outweighs the need for honesty. So, your villain must be absolutely certain that death is inevitable. They have abandoned all hope.

In the 1920s context, this often stems from psychological breaking points rather than logical choices.

Think of characters labeled with shell shock or those ruined by the economic shifts of the era. They view death as a release, not a punishment.

So, place this confession late in the story.

It validates what your sleuth has already deduced, but adds the emotional coloring that only the killer can provide.

The Ingenue with a Dark Side

She is the character least likely to be suspected.

And that is exactly why you use her.

We are talking about a young woman, perhaps a debutante or a companion, who exudes wide-eyed innocence. She plays the role of the "helpless female" perfectly, often acting as a ward or ally to your protagonist early in the story.

But beneath the tremulous facade, she is ruthless.

You want to lean into the 1920s ideal of sheltered femininity to mask her true nature. While the police dismiss her as too delicate for murder, she is likely observing everything and manipulating the investigation from the inside.

Give her a desperate, era-specific motive.

Perhaps she has secret gambling debts from a speakeasy or is frantically protecting a scandalous affair that would ruin her reputation.

The key is to drop subtle clues—like a knowing glance at a poison bottle or knowledge of a will she shouldn't have—before shattering her composure in the final act to reveal the cold calculator underneath.

The Gentleman Detective

This archetype offers a cerebral alternative to the hardboiled private eye.

He is defined by his intellect, his privilege, and his staggering lack of official authority.

And you need to use that privilege as a weapon.

Because of his high social standing and refined education, suspects don’t view him as a threat. They view him as "one of us." This allows him to slip into aristocratic circles—country estates, private clubs—where a working-class police inspector would be shut out.

While the police are bound by procedure, he operates on eccentricity.

Give him a niche obsession.

Whether it’s decoding medieval manuscripts or collecting rare poisons, this seemingly useless hobby should be the specific key that unlocks the puzzle.

His goal isn't to arrest the villain with a gun; it is to outthink them.

He succeeds specifically because he notices the details that the official authorities are too rigid to see.

The Spinster with a Secret Past

This character is the ultimate sleeper agent in your cast.

She appears to be your standard, unassuming middle-aged woman—perhaps a librarian, a companion, or just a quiet neighbor who enjoys her knitting. To the other suspects, she is invisible, a "superfluous woman" of the post-war era with nothing to offer but mild gossip.

But that is exactly why she is dangerous.

You want to contrast her mundane exterior with a dynamic, highly skilled history.

Perhaps she was a codebreaker for wartime intelligence, a nurse in the trenches, or a militant suffragette. Because she is underestimated, she can navigate the closed circle of a country house without raising alarms, gathering intel that the killer thinks is safe.

And when your protagonist hits a wall, she steps in.

Use her to provide a specialized solution based on her hidden past, such as decoding a cipher or identifying an obscure poison.

She acts as a mentor figure in a moment of crisis, offering the specific key needed to unlock the mystery without stealing the spotlight from your primary sleuth.

Social Satire

You can't write a 1920s mystery without a little bit of bite.

And that is where social satire comes in.

Essentially, you want to use wit to expose the cracks in the upper-class facade. While the aristocracy is strictly preaching propriety, your story should show them engaging in illicit affairs, hiding addictions, or scrambling for money.

This isn't just for laughs.

It serves a narrative purpose.

You should target their hypocrisy. Show a pompous host mocking the nouveau riche while he is secretly broke and terrified of losing his crumbling estate. The goal is to strip away the veneer of elegance to reveal the moral rot underneath.

And the best way to do this is through your protagonist.

Use their outsider perspective to poke fun at these rigid protocols. When a wealthy character makes a social error or snaps at a servant, let your sleuth clock it. It keeps the tone light and cozy, but it also provides the friction necessary to drive your plot forward.

Prohibition and Speakeasies

Prohibition isn't just historical window dressing; it is a structural engine for suspense.

And you need to use the inherent secrecy of the era.

By setting your scene in a speakeasy—whether a gritty basement requiring a password or a high-end club behind a false wall—you instantly create a confined, high-stakes environment.

This serves a specific function for the cozy mystery: it gives you a closed circle of suspects who are already hiding something.

Because the liquor is illicit and often poor quality, like bathtub gin masked by sweet mixers, it provides the perfect cover for a killer to slip poison into a drink unnoticed.

Lean into the contrast.

Use the setting to let your modern protagonist navigate the "glamour" of the Jazz Age, eavesdropping on whispered bootlegging deals while the police are busy raiding the wrong address.

It’s the perfect way to trap your characters in a web of lies, luxury, and danger.

War Trauma

You can't write about the 1920s without addressing the elephant in the room: World War I.

And specifically, the psychological toll it took on the men who came home.

In the era, they called it "shell shock."

And while this adds authentic historical depth, you need to use it as a functional tool for your mystery.

Give a character specific symptoms like tremors, a hypervigilance to loud noises, or sudden bouts of mutism.

This serves a critical purpose.

It creates a natural red herring. A suspect might be jittery, evasive, or prone to outbursts, making them look incredibly guilty. But in the end, it’s revealed they aren't the killer; they are simply struggling to reintegrate.

But be careful.

You want to balance the gravity of the trauma with the cozy tone of the genre. Avoid graphic flashbacks. Instead, use the trauma to humanize a secondary character or to give your empathetic sleuth a reason to look past the surface and find the truth.

templates.name: 1920s Historical Cozy Mystery Blurb
templates.content:
Book Description Template

Hook/Headline Block

Line 1: Craft a punchy high-concept premise, a rhetorical question related to the murder method/setting, or a triad of short, thematic fragments that establish the tone (e.g., humor, danger, mystery).

Line 2 (Optional): Use a stylized "Reader Review" snippet that highlights specific genre tropes (e.g., "unputdownable," "humorous," or "great setting") to provide immediate social proof and signal the "cozy" nature of the book.

Body Paragraph 1: The Setup and Inciting Incident

Sentence 1: Immediately ground the reader in the specific time period and setting (e.g., 1920s London, Egypt, Scottish Highlands) while introducing the protagonist’s status quo or profession.

Sentence 2: Contrast the protagonist's desire for a quiet life or their current social obligation (e.g., a ball, a restoration project, a new job) with a sudden, disruptive event.

Sentence 3: Introduce the inciting incident—usually the discovery of a body or a mysterious theft—linking it to a specific, intriguing location or object (e.g., a doorstep, a locked train compartment, a scribe's palette).

Sentence 4: Establish the immediate mystery hook by posing a question about the victim's identity, a missing object, or why the protagonist is personally drawn into the mess (reluctance vs. necessity).

Body Paragraph 2: The Complication and Investigation

Sentence 1: Define the protagonist’s active role as a sleuth, justifying why they are investigating instead of the police (e.g., protecting a family member, police incompetence, direct threat).

Sentence 2: Flesh out the "Cozy" atmosphere by listing the obstacles or specific genre elements the protagonist encounters, such as eccentric suspects, specific setting details (weather/architecture), or the friction of social etiquette.

Sentence 3: Introduce the "Sidekick" or "Ensemble" element—mentioning loyal maids, humorous pets, or romantic foils—to promise warmth and humor alongside the murder.

Sentence 4: Escalate the plot complexity by revealing that the initial crime is part of a larger web (e.g., forgeries, secret pasts, smugglers) or introducing distinct friction with an antagonist figure (like a grumpy Inspector).

Body Paragraph 3: The Escalation and Final Question

Sentence 1: Raise the stakes by introducing a "Ticking Clock" or a second escalation, such as another murder, a threat to the protagonist's safety, or a risk of wrongful execution for a loved one.

Sentence 2: Summarize the core conflict in a "David vs. Goliath" phrasing, contrasting the protagonist's amateur status or limited resources against the cunning of the killer.

Sentence 3: End the narrative section with a dramatic, open-ended question that challenges the protagonist's ability to solve the puzzle before a specific dire consequence occurs.

Outro Block

Line 1: Provide a snappy series summary that reinforces the brand keywords (e.g., "frolicking," "atmospheric," "humorous") and confirms the sub-genre.

Line 2: (Optional) Include a character "Bio/Branding" sentence if this is a series, reiterating their physical description, quirks, or backstory to build familiarity.

Line 3: explicit "For Fans Of" comparative statement, listing 2-3 popular authors in the niche to orient the algorithm and reader expectations.

Line 4: A direct Call to Action (CTA) instructing the reader to buy or download the book to solve the mystery.

templates.name: Bookstore Cozy Mystery Characters
templates.content:
Bookstore/Library Cozy Mysteries Character Arcs

The Intellectual Amateur Sleuth (Protagonist)

Character Arc: The protagonist begins the story seeking sanctuary or a fresh start in a bookish environment, often fleeing professional burnout, personal trauma, or the high-stress demands of city life. Initially, they attempt to maintain a low profile and rely on books or logic as a shield against the chaotic reality of their new small-town setting. However, when a murder disrupts their haven or threatens a loved one, they are forced to weaponize their specific professional skills—archival research, literary knowledge, or attention to detail—to investigate the crime. They transition from a passive observer who hides behind fiction to an active guardian of their community, ultimately realizing that justice requires confronting real-world danger rather than just reading about it.

Deepest Heart's Desire: They seek to establish a true sense of belonging and safety within a community that values their intellect. They want to protect the legacy of their bookstore or library, transforming it from a mere business into a permanent home where they are accepted for who they are.

Character Flaw: They suffer from emotional avoidance or imposter syndrome, frequently prioritizing intellectual analysis over emotional vulnerability. Their intense curiosity and "need to know" often override their sense of self-preservation, leading them to interfere in dangerous situations where they lack authority.

Character Demographics: Predominantly Female. Typically mid-30s to early 40s. Professional background often includes Librarian, Archivist, Editor, Academic, or specialized Retail/Business owner.

The Skeptical Guardian (Love Interest/Ally)

Character Arc: This character starts as a rigid figure of authority or a stoic local fixture who views the protagonist’s arrival and amateur sleuthing as an annoyance, a safety risk, or an interference with protocol. Whether a detective bound by the law or a local tradesman bound by grief and tradition, they initially erect emotional or professional walls to keep the protagonist at a distance. As the story progresses, they are humbled by the protagonist’s unique insights and ability to uncover clues that standard procedures missed. Their arc concludes with them breaking their own rules to protect the protagonist, shifting from an obstacle to a partner who values the protagonist's intuition as much as their own strength.

Deepest Heart's Desire: They desire order, stability, and the protection of their community from external chaos. Beneath their stoic exterior, they often yearn for a second chance at connection after a past loss (widower/divorce) or professional hardening.

Character Flaw: They can be dismissive, overly cautious, or emotionally emotionally unavailable due to past trauma. They tend to underestimate the capability of civilians (specifically the protagonist) and rely too heavily on established rules or "the safe choice" to navigate life.

Character Demographics: Male. Typically 30s to 40s. Profession usually involves Law Enforcement (Detective/Sheriff) or a grounding trade (Contractor/Real Estate/Landscaping).

The Loyal Sidekick (The Watson)

Character Arc: Often a family member (sister/cousin) or a spirited employee/best friend, this character begins the narrative in a state of dependency, eccentricity, or vulnerability, relying on the protagonist for stability. Throughout the investigation, they act as the catalyst for social interaction, pushing the introverted protagonist into community events where clues are gathered. They undergo a subtle transformation of empowerment, proving their worth by using their social networks or unexpected specific skills to crack a piece of the case the protagonist cannot. By the end, they move from a supporting player to an equal partner in the business or the investigation, securing their own independent happiness.

Deepest Heart's Desire: They crave excitement, validation, and a purposeful role within the protagonist's life and business. They want to see the protagonist succeed and be happy, often acting as a matchmaker or cheerleader to ensure the "ship" stays afloat.

Character Flaw: They can be overly trusting, gossip-prone, or lack the protagonist's filter, which frequently lands the duo in awkward or compromising social situations. Their enthusiasm sometimes blinds them to the physical danger of poking around a murder investigation.

Character Demographics: Usually Female. Age varies widely from peers (20s-30s) to older energetic retirees (60s+). Often hold roles like Assistant, Barista, relative, or eccentric retiree.

The Hidden Villain (The "Nice" Neighbor)

Character Arc: This character is introduced early as a benign, helpful, or sympathetic member of the community—often a customer, a grieving relative, or a "pillar of society." Throughout the narrative, they maintain a facade of cooperation, perhaps even offering the protagonist tea or advice while subtly steering suspicion toward others. Their arc is one of unmasking; as the protagonist digs into the past, the villain's friendly exterior cracks to reveal a desperate individual motivated by the preservation of a secret, reputation, or financial status. In the climax, they transform from a friend into a desperate threat, willing to destroy the protagonist to keep their past sins buried.

Deepest Heart's Desire: They desperately want to maintain the status quo and keep a long-buried secret (often regarding past academic fraud, illicit affairs, or old crimes) from destroying their current social standing. They seek control over the narrative of their life.

Character Flaw: Arrogance and self-preservation at the cost of human life. They believe their reputation or financial security is more valuable than the truth, leading them to justify increasingly violent acts as "necessary" to protect their lifestyle.

Character Demographics: Any gender, though often mirrors the protagonist in social standing. Age matches the timeline of the "past crime"—often middle-aged or elderly if the secret is old.

The Community Gatekeeper (The Gossip)

Character Arc: This character serves as the living memory of the small town, appearing as a nosy neighbor, a shop regular, or a busybody who knows everyone's history. Initially, they seem like a nuisance or a comic relief figure who impedes the protagonist's desire for privacy. However, as the mystery deepens, their role shifts from an annoyance to a critical information broker, providing the protagonist with oral history and social web connections that cannot be found in books. They eventually accept the protagonist into the inner circle, signaling the town's acceptance of the newcomer.

Deepest Heart's Desire: To be relevant, informed, and respected as an authority on the town's social hierarchy. They want to ensure that the town's history is remembered and that "outsiders" respect the local way of life.

Character Flaw: They are judgmental, prone to exaggeration, and have zero respect for boundaries or privacy. They can accidentally spread misinformation or put themselves in danger by knowing too much about the killer's business.

Character Demographics: Often Female. Typically older (60s-80s). Roles include long-time resident, shop owner, or retired professional.

The Sentient Companion (Animal Sidekick)

Character Arc: This character (usually a cat or dog) is attached to the bookstore or library and serves as a barometer for moral character. They begin by evaluating the protagonist's worthiness as the new caretaker of the space, offering comfort or aloofness. Throughout the story, they possess an almost supernatural intuition, growling at the hidden villain or physically uncovering clues (knocking over books, digging in gardens) that the human characters miss. Their arc concludes by physically intervening in the climax to protect the protagonist, solidifying their role as a partner rather than a pet.

Deepest Heart's Desire: To protect their territory (the shop/library) and comfort their chosen human. They seek a stable environment where routine is maintained and bad actors are expelled.

Character Flaw: They are governed by instinct and cannot communicate directly, leading to moments of frustration where the protagonist misunderstands their warnings. They can be chaotic agents, destroying property or creating messes that distract the protagonist at inopportune times.

Character Demographics: N/A (Cat or Dog). Often described with distinct personalities (grumpy, royal, energetic).

templates.name: Bookstore Cozy Mystery Plot
templates.content:
Bookstore/Library Cozy Mysteries Plot Template

Chapter 1: Establishing the Literary Haven

What Should Happen: The protagonist is introduced in their element within the bookstore or library setting, actively engaged in work that demonstrates their expertise and love of books—perhaps organizing inventory, preparing for a special event, or assisting a customer with a literary recommendation. The scene establishes the charm and atmosphere of the literary space while revealing the protagonist's personality through their actions rather than description. Supporting characters who work at or frequent the establishment are introduced naturally through their interactions with the protagonist. A minor conflict or concern is presented (business struggles, an upcoming event, or personal stress) that grounds the protagonist in reality before the inciting incident. The ordinary world of the bookstore or library is portrayed as a sanctuary of comfort and intellectual pursuit, creating a baseline of normalcy that the murder will later disrupt.

Chapter Notes:

Primary Purpose: Character introduction and establishing the status quo of the literary setting.

Multi-function: Yes—this scene introduces the protagonist, establishes the setting's atmosphere, introduces supporting characters, and sets up the business or professional context.

Structural Beats: Hook and Exposition; establishing the Ordinary World.

Ratings: Scene Intensity: 3, Spice Level: 1, Violence Level: 1, Swearing Level: 1.

Chapter 2: The Catalyst Event and Community Gathering

What Should Happen: The protagonist manages or participates in a significant community event at the bookstore or library—a book signing, author reading, book club meeting, or special literary celebration. This event brings together the key players who will become central to the mystery, including the eventual victim and primary suspects. Tensions, conflicts, or uncomfortable interactions occur during the gathering, planting seeds of motive and establishing relationships between characters that will become significant later. The victim is introduced while alive, allowing readers to form opinions about their character and observe their interactions with others. The event concludes with either the discovery of the body or a major disruption that sets the stage for the inciting incident, transforming what should have been a pleasant literary gathering into the catalyst for murder.

Chapter Notes:

Primary Purpose: Introducing the victim and suspects while advancing toward the inciting incident.

Multi-function: Yes—introduces key characters, establishes conflicts and motives, demonstrates community dynamics, and builds toward the murder discovery.

Structural Beats: Setup and foreshadowing; introducing the conflict.

Ratings: Scene Intensity: 6, Spice Level: 1, Violence Level: 2, Swearing Level: 2.

Chapter 3: Discovery of the Body

What Should Happen: The protagonist discovers the victim's body within or directly adjacent to the bookstore or library setting, typically in a location that feels integral to the literary space—in the stacks, near a reading area, in storage, or at the scene of the previous event. The discovery is handled without graphic violence, maintaining the cozy tone while making clear this was murder rather than accident or natural causes. The protagonist attempts to help or assess the situation, perhaps using a specific skill (CPR, first aid) that ultimately fails, raising the emotional stakes. Law enforcement is summoned immediately, and the protagonist must manage their shock while dealing with the practical reality that their beloved literary sanctuary has become a crime scene. The victim's final words, position, or the arrangement of books and objects near the body provide the first clues to the mystery.

Chapter Notes:

Primary Purpose: The Inciting Incident—the murder that launches the investigation.

Multi-function: Yes—provides the inciting incident, establishes the murder method, plants initial clues, and demonstrates the protagonist's immediate response to crisis.

Structural Beats: Inciting Incident; crossing from the Ordinary World into the adventure.

Ratings: Scene Intensity: 8, Spice Level: 1, Violence Level: 4, Swearing Level: 2.

Chapter 4: Official Investigation and Initial Questioning

What Should Happen: Law enforcement arrives to secure the crime scene and begins the official investigation, introducing the detective or police officer who will serve as the protagonist's professional contact throughout the case. The protagonist is questioned about their discovery of the body, their relationship to the victim, and their knowledge of events leading to the death. The official investigator's personality, competence level, and attitude toward amateur involvement is established—they may be dismissive, skeptical, or cautiously respectful of the protagonist. Practical complications arise regarding when the bookstore or library can reopen and what restrictions will be placed on the protagonist's access to their own space. The protagonist retreats with their closest ally or family member to process the shock, revealing vulnerabilities and backstory that explain their emotional investment in both the literary space and the need to find justice.

Chapter Notes:

Primary Purpose: Introducing law enforcement and establishing the official investigation parameters.

Multi-function: Yes—introduces the detective character, establishes procedural boundaries, reveals the protagonist's vulnerability, and sets up the tension between amateur and professional investigation.

Structural Beats: Reaction to the Inciting Incident; establishing the "rules" of the investigation.

Ratings: Scene Intensity: 6, Spice Level: 1, Violence Level: 2, Swearing Level: 2.

Chapter 5: Establishing Personal Stakes and Discovering Hidden Secrets

What Should Happen: The protagonist learns critical information that creates personal investment in solving the crime—perhaps a close friend or employee becomes a suspect, the murder threatens the bookstore or library's reputation and survival, or the victim's death is connected to a secret that could harm someone the protagonist cares about. While attempting to return to normal operations, the protagonist discovers a hidden element within the literary space—a secret room, locked drawer, hidden correspondence, or mysterious artifact—that connects to either the victim or the building's history. This discovery shifts the investigation from a purely external mystery to one that intersects with the protagonist's own legacy and the space they're trying to protect. The protagonist confides in their closest ally about their concerns and makes the decision to conduct their own quiet investigation alongside the official one.

Chapter Notes:

Primary Purpose: Establishing why the protagonist must personally investigate rather than leave it to police.

Multi-function: Yes—creates personal stakes, introduces a subplot or historical mystery, advances the worldbuilding of the setting, and shows the protagonist accepting the call to investigate.

Structural Beats: The Call to Adventure; establishing the B-story.

Ratings: Scene Intensity: 5, Spice Level: 1, Violence Level: 2, Swearing Level: 2.

Chapter 6: First Amateur Investigation—Gathering Intelligence

What Should Happen: The protagonist begins their investigation by leveraging their unique position within the literary community to gather information that official investigators cannot easily access. They conduct seemingly casual conversations with staff members, regular customers, or patrons while going about normal bookstore or library business, learning about the victim's recent activities, conflicts, and relationships. A literary clue is discovered—a book the victim was reading, a pattern in their borrowing or purchasing history, marginalia in a text, or a reference only someone knowledgeable about literature would understand. The protagonist's sidekick or closest ally is formally recruited as an investigative partner, and they begin organizing information, perhaps creating a suspect list or timeline.
